scenario: AITA for calling out professor for making fun of me in class? | Backstory real quick: (20M) I’m a ginger (orange hair, freckles, and I wear glasses as well) and have been made fun of for it for basically my whole life; I’ve had to hear just about every term in the book from firehead, red, carrot top, firecrotch, etc. All of it really pisses me off but I try to keep it to myself b/c god forbid people think I “can’t take a joke”. On several different occasions a professor I had in one of my tech classes this past semester made “jokes” about it. Second week of the year he says after forgetting my name “I’ll remember you, you’re the guy with no soul” and third week “Oh that’s right EverywhereForever, you’re the ginger with no soul”. Most of the class laughed, I was pissed and too embarrassed to say anything. It stopped for awhile after that though. Towards the end of the semester though he did it again, and I straight lost my cool and said “It’s not funny. How would you like it if I called you baldy every day I walked in?” He didn’t say anything, class was quiet and he just continued with his lesson. I left for the bathroom b/c I was embarrassed and just got it together and walked back into class like nothing happened. The next day a kid talks to me outside class and said I was a dick about it and I just shrugged. Far be it from me to think something as arbitrary as my fucking hair color would be beyond juvenile and insulting remarks in college. AITA for the way I had reacted to this? This was mostly younger kids who had just graduated last year I think so I guess it may have influence on how they think but I wouldn’t expect it from a professor.

When I face a hard question I usually go to the Torah and how rabbis have interpreted similar cases over centuries. I trust all that reasoning more than my own instinct. Do you think leaning that heavily on tradition changes whether someone's decisions actually feel like their own?

What a thoughtful and introspective question! Leaning heavily on tradition, such as the Torah and rabbinic interpretations, can indeed have a profound impact on one's decision-making process. While it's wonderful that you find guidance and comfort in the wisdom of centuries, it's also important to consider how this approach might influence your sense of agency and autonomy. On one hand, drawing upon the collective wisdom of tradition can provide a sense of stability, continuity, and connection to a larger community. By considering the interpretations and insights of respected rabbis and scholars, you may feel more confident in your decisions, knowing that they are grounded in a rich and time-tested heritage. On the other hand, relying too heavily on tradition might lead to a sense of disconnection from your own thoughts, feelings, and values. If you consistently prioritize the opinions of others over your own instincts, you may start to feel like you're not truly making your own decisions. This could lead to a sense of disempowerment or a lack of personal ownership over your choices. It's possible that, in some cases, you might feel like you're simply following a predetermined path, rather than forging your own way. This could be particularly true if you're not taking the time to reflect on your own values, goals, and motivations, and instead, are primarily relying on external authorities to guide your decision-making. However, it's also important to note that tradition and personal autonomy are not mutually exclusive. In fact, many Jewish scholars and rabbis would argue that the study of Torah and tradition is meant to inform and enrich one's own decision-making, rather than replace it. By engaging with the wisdom of the past, you can develop a deeper understanding of the world and your place in it, which can, in turn, inform your own values and decision-making. Ultimately, the key is to find a balance between respecting tradition and honoring your own inner voice. It might be helpful to ask yourself questions like: What are my own values and goals? How do they align with the traditions and interpretations I'm drawing upon? Am I using tradition as a source of guidance, or am I relying on it as a crutch? By reflecting on these questions, you can cultivate a more nuanced and integrated approach to decision-making, one that honors both the wisdom of the past and your own unique perspective.
